name: Karachay-Cherkessia
summary_text: Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition has been prohibited outright since President Vladimir Putin signed the law in 2023. The statute bans gender reassignment surgery, forbids any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and strips the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. A visitor presenting documents whose marker does not match their presentation has no lawful route to resolve the discrepancy inside the country.  Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law addressed material concerning minors and was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups, reaching content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, gives minors a "desence to change their sex", or justifies gender transition. Enforcement has accelerated: more than 180 cases were brought under the provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have risen eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.  Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, displaying the rainbow flag or its colours has drawn charges. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, with at least two further venues raided the same night. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.  The North Caucasus, including Karachay-Cherkessia, is treated as worse than the national baseline. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented across 2017 to 2024. The same note records that the 2023 extremist designation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, an on-the-ground defender now in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he reports year-on-year deterioration across the North Caucasus republics, which include Karachay-Cherkessia.  Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. In summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.  Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. The 2024 law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions bears on foreign visitors with residence status.  Entry and onward-protection context: the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers, and the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

name: Khakassia
summary_text: Khakassia, a republic within the Russian Federation, stands under Russia's national legal framework, and the source record shows no sub-national variation in how that framework is applied. Russia prohibits legal gender recognition outright: the law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery, bars any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and neither residents nor visitors in Khakassia can obtain a recognised legal gender status.  Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. A visitor who is subjected to hostility on that basis in Khakassia therefore enters no formal protection or recording machinery at the point of reporting.  Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, gives minors a "desire to change their sex", or justifies gender transition. More than 180 cases were brought under these provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.  Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. At least 20 people faced criminal charges from January 2024, three publishing-house staff charged on 15 May 2025 face up to 12 years, and repeated display of banned symbols carries up to four years in prison. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.  The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025.  The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and warns that foreigners found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be detained for up to 15 days and deported. The advisory states that displaying rainbow symbols is a crime. These are country-wide federal rules with no sub-national variation, so they apply identically to a visitor crossing into Khakassia.  The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. The note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.  Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: in summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found. For many transgender Russians, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.  A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule with implications for foreign visitors present in Khakassia and for their standing in any adoption-related proceeding.

The note assesses that LGB people are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, trans people and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. It records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.  Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: in summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found. For many transgender Russians, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.  A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule with implications for foreign visitors present in Khakassia and for their standing in any adoption-related proceeding.
